summary: An excerpt from a fiction work ("Book 1 — part 99") in which a speaker recounts the 1960s Berkeley student activism that followed Freedom Rider recruitment at campus tables near Bancroft and Telegraph Avenue. It describes the campus free speech fight, the rise of radical student and identity-based movements, and the playful, media-savvy Yippies, including their 1968 Chicago Democratic National Convention protests. The passage ends mid-sentence as the Yippies' slogan "Never trust anyone over 30" is being explained.
one_line: A fictional character recounts Berkeley's Free Speech Movement and the playful Yippies' 1968 Chicago convention protests.
key_facts: Freedom Riders were recruited from information tables on campus at Bancroft and Telegraph Avenue.
The university president banned political organizing on campus, but civil rights students did not stop.
When police arrested a guy handing out literature, 3,000 students surrounded the van and refused to let it budge.
The confrontation over the arrest galvanized the Free Speech Movement, described as the start of the hippies.
Radical offshoots of the movement included Black power groups like the Black Panthers, gay rights groups like the Pink Panthers, and radical women's groups including lesbian separatists.
The Yippies were described as very political hippies who were playful pranksters rather than serious politicians.
The Yippies threw money into the New York Stock Exchange.
Yippies circled the Pentagon with hundreds of protestors and said a magic spell supposed to levitate it.
The Yippies invented a fictional kind of LSD that was sprayed onto people with squirt-guns.
The clown Wavy Gravy got hundreds of protestors to dress up as Santa Claus so cameras would show police arresting Santa.
The Yippies' big moment was the Democratic National Convention in 1968 in Chicago, where they protested the Vietnam War.
Yippies ran a pig called Pigasus for the presidential nomination.
Police attacked reporters at the Chicago demonstrations, and the reporters showed the beatings on television.
The Chicago violence was called a 'police riot.'
The Yippies' slogan was 'Never trust anyone over 30.'
